title: Chanting in Zen
hook: the Heart Sutra, the four vows, the names of the ancestors

segments.voice: Yesterday: the han, the wooden board that calls the hall to sit, and reminds it that life is short. Your line: time passes swiftly.

Zen has a reputation for silence, so the morning service can come as a surprise. Before breakfast, the whole hall stands or kneels and chants, loudly, in one low, steady pitch. A hollow wooden drum, carved in the shape of a fish, keeps the beat: tok, tok, tok. Nobody is performing. Nobody is singing harmony. Voices that don't match blend into one sound that seems to fill the floorboards. Then it stops, and the silence afterward feels different.
screen: `A SILENT SCHOOL THAT CHANTS.` → `ONE LOW PITCH, ONE BEAT.` → `THE SILENCE AFTER.`

segments.voice: First, the Heart Sutra. You met it earlier on this path: the short text where Avalokiteshvara sees that all five heaps are empty, and tells Shariputra that form is emptiness and emptiness is form. Zen halls chant it often, in Japanese, Chinese, Korean, Vietnamese or English, depending on the community. Chanting it isn't studying it. The aim is to let the text pass through the body until it's breath, not argument. Second, the four vows: the bodhisattva vows, said together, often at the end of a service. In plain paraphrase: beings are without number, I vow to free them. Delusions never run out, I vow to end them. The gates of the teaching are without limit, I vow to enter them. The Buddha's way is beyond reach, I vow to embody it. Each vow names something impossible, and promises it anyway. Third, the ancestors. Some services chant the lineage: the Buddha, then teacher after teacher, down to the founders of that community's line. A family tree said aloud, a reminder that this practice came hand to hand, through people. Fourth, one voice, one body. Chanting uses breath, belly and throat. It's hard to chant at full voice and think about lunch. And chanting together makes the hall one body, the way kinhin made it one line. Zen silence and Zen chanting aren't opposites. Both are ways of being entirely here.
screen: `THE HEART SUTRA, AS BREATH.` · `FOUR VOWS, EACH IMPOSSIBLE.` · `THE ANCESTORS, NAME BY NAME.` · `ONE VOICE, ONE BODY.` · then, large: `CHANTING ZEN.`

segments.voice: Sit up and take a full breath into the belly. If you practice, say the four vows in your community's wording; if not, say today's plain paraphrase slowly, in one low, steady tone, from beings are without number through all four, without worrying about perfect words. Then sit in the quiet that follows.
Chanting in Zen. The Heart Sutra, the four vows and the names of the ancestors, chanted together in one low voice, as practice for the whole body. Today's word.
Your line: chanting zen. Voices that don't match, blended into one low sound. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Zen communities hold chanting services, often morning and evening, where the Heart Sutra, the four bodhisattva vows, dedications and sometimes the names of the lineage ancestors are chanted together in a steady tone, often kept in time by a wooden drum.

chat.says: I thought Zen was all silence. Why do they chant so loudly?
options: Chanting takes the whole body and joins the hall in one voice; like silence, it's being fully here.
It's mostly a warm-up to wake people up before the real practice of silence begins.
It's a performance for visitors, to show off the temple's music and its old texts.
